notes.definition: Radio waves can be produced by oscillating currents in electrical circuits, and when absorbed they can induce an alternating current of the same frequency (Higher). Changes in atoms and nuclei also generate and absorb EM waves; gamma rays come from changes in the nucleus. Ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays can harm body tissue, and radiation dose (in sieverts) measures the risk of harm.
explanation: Higher tier: radio waves can be produced by oscillations in electrical circuits. In a radio transmitter, an alternating current makes electrons oscillate up and down the aerial. This produces radio waves with the same frequency as the oscillating current. When radio waves reach a receiving aerial they are absorbed, and they make the electrons in the aerial oscillate. This creates an alternating current with the same frequency as the radio wave itself. So radio waves can induce oscillations in an electrical circuit, which is how a radio, television or phone picks up a signal.

EM waves are also generated or absorbed when changes happen inside atoms and nuclei. When electrons in atoms move between energy levels they can emit or absorb visible light, ultraviolet or X-rays, for example. Changes in the nucleus of an atom produce gamma rays: gamma rays originate from the nucleus. Because of the wide range of possible changes, atoms and nuclei can generate and absorb EM radiation over a very wide range of frequencies.

Ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays are high-frequency EM waves that carry a lot of energy and can damage human body tissue. Ultraviolet can cause the skin to age prematurely and increases the risk of skin cancer; it can also cause sunburn and damage the eyes. X-rays and gamma rays are ionising radiation: they can knock electrons out of atoms, which can cause mutation of genes (changes to DNA) and lead to cancer. The effects depend on the type of radiation and the size of the dose.

Radiation dose, measured in sieverts (Sv), is a measure of the risk of harm resulting from exposure of the body to radiation. One sievert is a very large dose, so doses are usually given in millisieverts: 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv). As a guide, the average yearly dose from background radiation in the UK is about 2.7 mSv, a chest X-ray gives about 0.02 mSv and a CT scan can give about 10 mSv. You do not need to recall the unit, but you must be able to use data about doses to draw conclusions about risks and consequences of exposure.

When evaluating risk from data, compare the doses involved, consider how often the exposure happens and weigh the benefit (such as diagnosing an illness) against the risk. A higher dose means a greater risk of harm. For example, if a CT scan gives 500 times the dose of a chest X-ray, a doctor will only order it when the extra information is worth the higher risk.
keyFacts: Higher: radio waves can be produced by oscillations (alternating currents) in electrical circuits.
Higher: absorbed radio waves can induce an alternating current with the same frequency as the radio wave.
Changes in atoms and nuclei can generate or absorb EM waves over a wide frequency range.
Gamma rays originate from changes in the nucleus of an atom.
UV can make skin age prematurely and increases the risk of skin cancer.
X-rays and gamma rays are ionising and can cause mutation of genes and cancer.
Effects depend on the type of radiation and the size of the dose.
Radiation dose (sieverts, Sv) measures the risk of harm from exposure.

keyTerms.definition: A repeated back and forth movement; in a circuit, an alternating current that changes direction regularly.
A conductor that emits radio waves when a current oscillates in it, or absorbs them to produce a current.
Radiation with enough energy to remove electrons from atoms, such as X-rays and gamma rays.
A change in the genetic material (DNA) of a cell, which can lead to cancer.
A measure of the risk of harm resulting from exposure of the body to radiation, measured in sieverts (Sv).
The unit of radiation dose; 1 Sv = 1000 mSv.

workedExamples.title: Converting dose units
workedExamples.question: A patient receives a dose of 0.0027 Sv. Convert this to millisieverts.

workedExamples.title: Comparing risks from data
workedExamples.question: A chest X-ray gives a dose of 0.02 mSv and a CT scan gives 10 mSv. How many chest X-rays give the same dose as one CT scan, and what does this suggest about risk?
steps: The CT scan dose is 500 times larger.
A larger dose means a greater risk of harm (cancer), so a CT scan should only be used when its benefit justifies the higher risk.
workedExamples.answer: 500 chest X-rays; the CT scan carries a much greater risk.

workedExamples.title: Higher: frequency of the induced current
workedExamples.question: A radio aerial absorbs radio waves of frequency 100 MHz. State the frequency of the alternating current induced and calculate the wavelength of the waves. (speed = 3 × 10⁸ m/s)
steps: The induced alternating current has the same frequency as the radio wave: 100 MHz = 1 × 10⁸ Hz.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the current induced in a receiving aerial has a different frequency from the radio wave.
misconceptions.right: In fact the alternating current has the same frequency as the radio wave that induced it.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think all EM radiation is ionising and causes cancer.
misconceptions.right: In fact only the high-frequency end (some UV, X-rays and gamma rays) is ionising. Radio waves and visible light are not.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a sievert is a small unit.
misconceptions.right: In fact 1 Sv is a very large dose; most doses are measured in millisieverts (1000 mSv = 1 Sv).

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think gamma rays come from the electrons in an atom.
misconceptions.right: In fact gamma rays originate from changes in the nucleus.

realWorld: Radio and television transmitters use oscillating currents in tall aerials to broadcast signals; your radio's aerial turns them back into a current.
Hospitals record patients' radiation doses in millisieverts and limit the number of X-rays and CT scans.
Sunscreen and sunglasses protect skin and eyes from ultraviolet radiation.
Radiographers stand behind lead screens and wear dosimeters to monitor their dose.
higherTier: Radio waves can be produced by oscillations in electrical circuits.
When radio waves are absorbed they may create an alternating current with the same frequency as the radio wave, so radio waves can induce oscillations in an electrical circuit.
Note: the content on atoms and nuclei, hazards of UV, X-rays and gamma rays, and radiation dose in sieverts is for both tiers.
examTips: Higher: always say the induced alternating current has the SAME frequency as the radio wave.
Link each hazard to the right radiation: UV → premature skin ageing and skin cancer; X-rays and gamma → ionising, gene mutation, cancer.
Convert between Sv and mSv carefully: multiply by 1000 to go from Sv to mSv.
When asked to draw conclusions from dose data, compare the numbers (for example, 'about 500 times larger') and link a larger dose to a larger risk.
Remember gamma rays come from the nucleus; this links to radioactive decay in the atomic structure topic.
summary: Higher: oscillating currents produce radio waves.
Higher: absorbed radio waves induce an AC of the same frequency.
Atoms and nuclei emit and absorb EM waves; gamma rays come from the nucleus.
UV: skin ageing and skin cancer; X-rays and gamma: ionising, mutations and cancer.
Harm depends on radiation type and dose.
Dose in sieverts measures risk; 1000 mSv = 1 Sv.

questions.question: How can radio waves be produced?
options: By heating an object until it glows
By changes in the nucleus of an atom
By oscillating currents in an electrical circuit
By vibrating air particles
markScheme: 1 mark: By oscillating currents in an electrical circuit
questions.explanation: Radio waves are produced by oscillations in electrical circuits, such as an alternating current in a transmitter aerial. Changes in nuclei produce gamma rays; vibrating air is sound.

questions.question:
Radio waves of frequency 200 kHz are absorbed by an aerial.
What is the frequency of the alternating current induced in the aerial?
options: 200 kHz
100 kHz
400 kHz
50 Hz
markScheme: 1 mark: 200 kHz
questions.explanation: The induced alternating current has the same frequency as the radio wave that produced it: 200 kHz.

questions.question: Where do gamma rays originate?
options: From oscillating electrons in an aerial
From hot objects such as heaters
From electrons moving between energy levels in atoms only
From changes in the nucleus of an atom
markScheme: 1 mark: From changes in the nucleus of an atom
questions.explanation: Gamma rays come from changes in the nucleus, for example during radioactive decay.

questions.question: Which effect is caused by excessive exposure of the skin to ultraviolet radiation?
options: Heating of internal organs
Premature ageing of the skin
Mutation caused by radio waves
Loss of hearing
markScheme: 1 mark: Premature ageing of the skin
questions.explanation: UV can cause skin to age prematurely and increases the risk of skin cancer.

questions.question: What is the unit of radiation dose?
options: Hertz (Hz)
Sievert (Sv)
Becquerel (Bq)
Watt (W)
markScheme: 1 mark: Sievert (Sv)
questions.explanation: Radiation dose is measured in sieverts. The becquerel is the unit of activity, which is a different quantity.

questions.question: Which statement about X-rays and gamma rays is correct?
options: They are harmless because they pass straight through the body
They only affect the surface of the skin
They cause harm only by heating tissue
They are ionising and can cause mutation of genes and cancer
markScheme: 1 mark: They are ionising and can cause mutation of genes and cancer
questions.explanation: X-rays and gamma rays are ionising radiation. They can damage DNA, causing gene mutations and cancer.

questions.question: What does radiation dose measure?
options: The risk of harm from exposure of the body to radiation
The number of nuclei that decay each second
The frequency of the radiation
The time taken for half the nuclei to decay
markScheme: 1 mark: The risk of harm from exposure of the body to radiation
questions.explanation: Dose (in sieverts) is a measure of the risk of harm. Activity and half-life are different quantities.

questions.question: How many millisieverts (mSv) are there in 1 sievert (Sv)?
markScheme: 1 mark: 1000
questions.explanation: 1000 mSv = 1 Sv, because 'milli' means one thousandth.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the radiation dose a patient receives from two medical scans.
How many times larger is the dose from scan B than the dose from scan A?
options: 10 times
1000 times
0.1 times
100 times
markScheme: 1 mark: 100 times
questions.explanation: 0.05 Sv = 50 mSv. 50 ÷ 0.5 = 100, so the second dose is 100 times larger.

questions.question: Which statement explains how a radio receiver detects a radio signal?
options: Radio waves are converted directly into sound waves by the aerial
Radio waves produce a direct current in the aerial
Radio waves are absorbed by the aerial and make electrons oscillate, creating an alternating current
Radio waves make the nuclei in the aerial emit gamma rays
markScheme: 1 mark: Radio waves are absorbed by the aerial and make electrons oscillate, creating an alternating current
questions.explanation: Absorbed radio waves induce oscillations of the electrons, which is an alternating current at the same frequency as the wave. The receiver then processes this signal.

questions.question:
A person receives a radiation dose of 2.7 mSv.
What is this dose in sieverts?
markScheme: 1 mark: 0.0027 Sv
questions.explanation: Divide by 1000 to go from mSv to Sv: 2.7 ÷ 1000 = 0.0027 Sv.

questions.question:
A worker receives a radiation dose of 0.05 Sv.
What is this dose in millisieverts?
markScheme: 1 mark: 50 mSv
questions.explanation: Multiply by 1000: 0.05 × 1000 = 50 mSv.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the radiation dose from two medical procedures.
Calculate how many chest X-rays would give the same total dose as one CT scan.
markScheme: 1 mark: 500
questions.explanation: 10 ÷ 0.02 = 500. The CT scan dose is 500 times greater, so it carries a much greater risk.

questions.question:
The average radiation dose from background radiation in the UK is 2.7 mSv per year.
There are 365 days in one year.
Calculate the average dose per day.
Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
markScheme: 1 mark: 0.0074 mSv

questions.question:
An oscillating current of frequency 1.0 MHz in a transmitter aerial produces radio waves.
The speed of radio waves is 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.
Calculate the wavelength of the radio waves.
markScheme: 1 mark: 300 m
questions.explanation: The radio waves have the same frequency as the oscillating current, 1.0 × 10⁶ Hz. λ = v ÷ f = 300 m.

questions.question:
Radio waves of frequency 100 MHz induce an alternating current in an aerial.
Calculate the period of the alternating current.
Use the equation:
period = 1 ÷ frequency
Give your answer in standard form.
markScheme: 1 mark: f = 100 MHz = 1 × 10⁸ Hz, T = 1 ÷ 1 × 10⁸
1 mark: 1 × 10⁻⁸ s
questions.explanation: The current has the same frequency as the radio wave. T = 1/f = 1 ÷ 1 × 10⁸ = 1 × 10⁻⁸ s.

questions.question: Give two factors that determine how harmful a dose of radiation is to body tissue.
markScheme: 1 mark: the type of radiation
1 mark: the size of the dose
questions.explanation: The spec states that effects depend on the type of radiation and the size of the dose.

questions.question: Explain why people should use sunscreen in strong sunlight.
markScheme: 1 mark: sunlight contains ultraviolet radiation
1 mark: which can cause premature skin ageing / increase the risk of skin cancer; sunscreen absorbs or reflects UV
questions.explanation: Sunscreen reduces the UV reaching the skin and so reduces the risk.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the radiation dose from two medical procedures.
Use data from Table 1 to compare the risks of the two procedures.
Suggest why doctors still use CT scans.
markScheme: 1 mark: the CT dose is 2000 times larger (10 ÷ 0.005)
1 mark: so the CT scan has a much greater risk of harm / cancer
1 mark: used when the benefit (diagnosing a serious condition) outweighs the risk
questions.explanation: Drawing conclusions from data means calculating a comparison and weighing benefit against risk.

questions.question: Name what can be generated or absorbed when changes happen in atoms and in the nuclei of atoms.
markScheme: 1 mark: electromagnetic waves / radiation (over a wide frequency range)
questions.explanation: Changes in atoms and nuclei generate or absorb EM waves; nuclear changes produce gamma rays.

markScheme: Indicative content:
an alternating current in the transmitter circuit makes electrons oscillate in the transmitter aerial
this produces radio waves of the same frequency
radio waves (EM waves) travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s to the receiver
the receiving aerial absorbs the radio waves
electrons in the receiving aerial oscillate, inducing an alternating current
the induced current has the same frequency as the radio wave
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): links oscillating current, radio waves and induced AC with the same frequency.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about transmitters or receivers.
questions.explanation: Production and absorption of radio waves are reverse processes; the frequency is the same throughout.

questions.question:
Hospitals use X-rays and gamma rays in medicine.
Table 1 shows typical radiation doses.
Explain the hazards of ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays to the human body.
Explain how radiation dose data can be used to judge the risk of a medical procedure.

rows: Background radiation in one year (UK average)

markScheme: Indicative content:
UV, X-rays and gamma are high-frequency EM waves that transfer a lot of energy
UV: causes premature ageing of skin and increases risk of skin cancer (also sunburn, eye damage)
X-rays and gamma rays: ionising radiation
ionisation can damage DNA, causing mutation of genes, which can lead to cancer
harm depends on the type of radiation and the size of the dose
radiation dose (in sieverts) is a measure of the risk of harm
1000 mSv = 1 Sv; typical doses quoted in mSv
compare doses, e.g. CT scan about 10 mSv versus chest X-ray about 0.02 mSv
larger dose means greater risk; risk must be weighed against the medical benefit
limit number of scans; protect staff (lead screens, distance, dosimeters)
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): detailed explanation of hazards for each type and clear use of dose data to judge risk.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): describes hazards and refers to dose and risk with limited use of data.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements that radiation is harmful.
questions.explanation: A full answer links each radiation to its effect and explains dose as a measure of risk.

questions.question: Which conclusion about radiation dose is correct?
options: A dose of 10 mSv is ten times larger than a dose of 1 Sv
Two scans of 5 mSv each carry a similar risk to one scan of 10 mSv
Dose measures how quickly a source decays
Any dose below 1 Sv carries no risk at all
markScheme: 1 mark: Two scans of 5 mSv each carry a similar risk to one scan of 10 mSv
questions.explanation: Dose is a measure of risk, so the same total dose gives a similar risk. 1 Sv = 1000 mSv, so 10 mSv is much smaller than 1 Sv, and even small doses carry some risk.

questions.question:
Radiographers take many X-ray images each day.
Each patient receives only a small radiation dose.
Explain why radiographers stand behind a lead screen when taking X-ray images.
markScheme: 1 mark: the radiographer would be exposed many times, so their total dose (and risk) would build up
1 mark: lead absorbs X-rays, reducing their dose and risk of cancer / gene mutation
questions.explanation: Patients have occasional scans, but staff would receive repeated doses without shielding.
